analysis.one_liner: Bans making, using, and selling asbestos, phasing it out of chlorine plants.
analysis.headline: The asbestos ban bill drew 37 cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote in the House committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would ban the manufacture, processing, use, and sale of commercial asbestos and products containing it, effective one year after passage. It would give plants that use asbestos to make chlorine a two-year window to switch to other methods, allow the President to grant national-security exemptions, and require the EPA to publish public education materials about asbestos health risks. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families who are exposed to asbestos on the job or through products — asbestos causes cancer and other fatal diseases, and this would shut off new exposure at the source. Consumers, schoolchildren, and building occupants also gain, since fewer asbestos-containing products would enter buildings and homes. It also directs the EPA to create public materials explaining asbestos health risks and how to find licensed asbestos-removal services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, families, and communities exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Bans the manufacture, processing, use, and sale of commercial asbestos and any product containing it, effective one year after enactment — cutting off new asbestos exposure at the source.
Defines commercial asbestos to cover all eight known asbestos fiber types, including chrysotile, the type still imported and used in the United States.
Requires the EPA to develop public education resources on the health effects of asbestos exposure and the availability of licensed asbestos mitigation services in every state.
Closes a loophole by barring the EPA Administrator from issuing waivers that would let companies off the hook from the asbestos rules.

analysis.who_pays: A small group of chlor-alkali (chlorine-producing) plants that still use asbestos diaphragms would have to import and buy asbestos at most two more years and then pay to convert to non-asbestos technology. Companies that import or sell asbestos and the manufacturers of products containing it would lose their market. Any transition costs could show up modestly in the price of chlorine-based products.

drawbacks.text: Plants that use asbestos diaphragms to make chlorine get only a two-year runway to convert to alternative technology, which imposes real conversion costs on those facilities and could slightly raise prices for chlorine-based products during the transition.

The ban does nothing about asbestos already installed in older buildings — the bill expressly excludes the ongoing end-use of asbestos products already in place — so exposure risks in older homes, schools, and workplaces would persist and still require costly removal.
The President could grant national-security exemptions lasting up to three years, extendable once, which in theory could stretch out the ban for particular users.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and durable: a legal ban on a substance that causes fatal cancers, affecting workers and the public for decades. The costs fall on a small, identifiable set of chlorine plants with a defined phase-out window, and on importers of a product most of the world has already abandoned. This is a bill where the benefit clearly outweighs the cost; the main honest caveat is that it addresses only new asbestos, not the asbestos already sitting in older buildings.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On April 7, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials — the last action it ever received.
The bill gathered 37 cosponsors, 36 Democrats and 1 Republican, but the committee never held a markup or brought it to the House floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The chlor-alkali plants that still use asbestos diaphragms and the companies that import and sell asbestos are better off, because no ban was enacted and they can keep operating under the weaker existing regulatory process. Anyone with a stake in the status quo avoided a floor vote.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 37 cosponsors.

for.name: 37 House cosponsors (36 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of a full asbestos ban.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — across the entire 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic — 36 of 37 cosponsors were Democrats — and the Republican-controlled committee that held the bill took no action on it.

industries.industry: Chlor-alkali (chlorine and alkali producers using asbestos diaphragms)
industries.note: A handful of US chlorine plants still import chrysotile asbestos to make diaphragms for chlorine production. The bill would end that after a two-year grace period, forcing conversion to non-asbestos technology; keeping asbestos in use keeps workers and nearby communities exposed.
The bill bans importing, processing, and distributing commercial asbestos, eliminating their US market.

industries.industry: Licensed asbestos abatement and removal contractors
industries.note: The bill requires the EPA to publish public education materials that include how to find licensed asbestos mitigation services in each state, which would steer more property owners toward licensed removal.
